name: Muhammad
info: Muhammad was an Arab religious, military and political leader of Mecca and Medina in the early 7th century, whom Muslims hold to be the final prophet of God and whose reported revelations form the Quran.

facts.born: c. 570 in Mecca, in the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh, son of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Amina bint Wahb
facts.died: 8 June 632 in Medina, after an illness of some days; buried where he died, in Aisha's house, later included in the Prophet's Mosque
facts.role: Founder of Islam; held by Muslims to be the Seal of the Prophets, the last prophet sent by God; leader of the Muslim community in Medina from 622 and of most of Arabia by 632
facts.known: the revelations that form the Quran; the Hijrah to Medina in 622; the Constitution of Medina; the Battle of Badr; the conquest of Mecca; the Farewell Pilgrimage; the sunnah preserved in the hadith

t: Born into the Quraysh of Mecca and orphaned young, Muhammad reported in about 610 that he had received the first of the revelations that Muslims hold to be the word of God, and began preaching publicly in 613.

After 13 years of persecution in Mecca he and his followers migrated to Medina in 622, the event that began the Islamic calendar, and there he led a community that grew through treaties, raids and wars.
By his death on 8 June 632 most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam, and the dispute over who should succeed him shaped the later division between Sunni and Shia Muslims.
dyk: The Quran contains comparatively little direct information about Muhammad himself, although it names him in several verses and briefly refers to episodes such as the migration to Yathrib and the Battle of Badr.
ev: Muhammad is born in Mecca into the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh
He reports a visit from Gabriel in the cave of Hira and the first revelation
The Hijrah: he and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina
The Muslims win the Battle of Badr against a larger Meccan force
The Treaty of Hudaybiyya establishes a ten-year truce with the Quraysh
He marches on Mecca with 10,000 men and takes the city with minimal casualties
He leads the Farewell Pilgrimage and dies in Medina on 8 June

sections.early:
According to the traditional account, Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 into the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh, then a dominant force in western Arabia. His father, Abdullah, died almost six months before he was born, and his mother, Amina, died when he was six. He was cared for by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib until the latter's death, then by his uncle Abu Talib, the new leader of the clan, and he later led caravans on the route to Syria for another uncle, Abbas.

The historical record of Mecca in these years is limited and fragmentary, which makes it hard to separate fact from legend. Several Islamic narratives tell of a boyhood journey to Syria and a meeting with the monk Bahira, who foretold his prophethood; modern historians, and some medieval Muslim scholars such as al-Dhahabi, have judged all accounts of Bahira to be fictitious. At about 25 he married Khadija, a wealthy merchant of about 40 who had hired him to take a caravan to Syria, and he remained monogamous until her death. In 605, by a narrative collected by Ibn Ishaq, he settled a dispute among the clans over who should set the Black Stone back into the rebuilt Kaaba.
sections.rise:
According to Islamic tradition, in 610, when he was 40, the angel Gabriel appeared to Muhammad in the cave of Hira, where he sometimes withdrew for prayer, and instructed him to read; the first verses delivered are held to be Quran 96:1-5. The traditional account says he came down from the mountain frightened and that Khadija reassured him, as did her Christian cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal. Muslim tradition holds that Khadija was the first to believe, followed by his ten-year-old cousin Ali ibn Abi Talib, his friend Abu Bakr and his adopted son Zayd.

Muhammad was at first reluctant to speak of the revelations and confided in a few relatives and friends. Around 613 he began to preach publicly, proclaiming that God is One, that complete submission (Islam) to God is the right way of life, and that he was a prophet and messenger of God. Many early followers were women, freedmen, servants and slaves, who memorised each new revelation as he recited it. He introduced prayer with physical postures of submission and almsgiving (zakat) as a duty of the community (ummah). The Quraysh at first took little notice, but tensions grew once he attacked their beliefs.
sections.deeds:
In 622, after pledges at Aqaba from men of Medina, Muhammad called on the Meccan Muslims to move to Medina, and arrived there with Abu Bakr on 4 September 622. The Hijrah marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. In Medina the Muslims built a mosque that served as his residence and a place for prayer, public meetings and the care of the poor, and Bilal, a former Abyssinian slave, was chosen to call the community to prayer. Muhammad also set down the text commonly called the Constitution of Medina, in which the Arab and Jewish tribes of the oasis promised to live in peace with the Muslims and to defend Medina if attacked; scholars dispute whether it was a treaty or a unilateral proclamation.

War with the Quraysh followed. At Badr in March 624 some three hundred Muslims defeated a larger Meccan force, killing at least forty-five Meccans for the loss of fourteen. The Muslims were beaten at Uhud in 625 and withstood a siege of Medina, behind a trench, in 627. In 628 the Treaty of Hudaybiyya set a ten-year truce, and in 630 Muhammad marched on Mecca with 10,000 men, took the city with minimal casualties, declared an amnesty with a few exceptions and destroyed the statues of the Arabian gods around the Kaaba. In 632 he led the Farewell Pilgrimage and preached a sermon.
sections.opponents:
In Mecca, Muhammad's opponents were chiefly the Quraysh leaders, who said he had derided their ancestors and gods and divided their community. Contemporaries also accused him of being possessed by a jinn, a soothsayer or a magician. His uncle Abu Talib protected him but did not accept Islam. In 616 the other Quraysh clans agreed to a ban on trade and marriage with the Banu Hashim, lifted in 619. After Khadija and Abu Talib died in 619, he sought support in Ta'if, where, according to the account, he was rejected and stoned.

The Medinan years are told with episodes of violence that sources and scholars treat differently. The Banu Qaynuqa and the Banu Nadir were expelled from Medina after sieges, and after the Battle of the Trench the Banu Qurayza surrendered. By Ibn Ishaq's account the men were beheaded and the women and children enslaved, with the judgement given by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, whom Muhammad approved; Walid N. Arafat and Barakat Ahmad dispute that account, and Meir J. Kister has argued against them in turn. Criticism of him has existed since the 7th century and now questions his legitimacy as a prophet, his conduct, his marriages, his ownership of slaves and his treatment of enemies; Western and Byzantine Christians of the Middle Ages called him a false prophet.
sections.last:
In June 632, after praying at a burial site, Muhammad suffered a severe headache. He spent his illness moving among his wives' rooms, and asked to stay in Aisha's, walking there with the help of Ali and Fadl ibn Abbas. According to various sources, including Sahih al-Bukhari, he said he felt his aorta being severed because of the food he had eaten at Khaybar, where a meal was said to have been poisoned. He died on 8 June 632, and his last words are reported as a prayer: "O God, forgive me and have mercy on me; and let me join the highest companions." The historian Alfred T. Welch, who presumes the illness to have been an ordinary Medinan fever, limits his speculation to physical and mental fatigue.

He was buried where he died, in Aisha's house, which was later included in the Prophet's Mosque. The question of a successor divided the community at once. Umar ibn al-Khattab nominated Abu Bakr, who was confirmed as the first caliph. Some companions disputed this choice, holding that Muhammad had designated his cousin and son-in-law Ali ibn Abi Talib as successor at Ghadir Khumm. This dispute is the origin of the later division between Sunni and Shia. Within a decade the Muslims had conquered Mesopotamia, Byzantine Syria and Egypt and large parts of Persia.
sections.legacy:
In Islamic belief Muhammad is the last prophet sent by God, and the Shahada declares that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is a Messenger of God. The revelations he reported form the Quran, which Muslims regard as the verbatim word of God. His teachings and practices, preserved in hadith and in his biography (sirah), form the sunnah, a model for Muslims and a source of Islamic law; many details of the daily prayers, the fast and the pilgrimage are found only there. Sufi orders trace their spiritual descent to him, and his birthday is celebrated as a major feast in much of the Muslim world. Muslims commonly follow his name with a blessing, and generally avoid depicting him, instead using calligraphy such as the hilya.

He is also honoured in other faiths: as one of the seven main prophets of the Druze faith, as a Manifestation of God in the Baha'i Faith, and by Sikhs as one of the divine messengers. Historians depend on sources written in the 8th and 9th centuries, and John Burton judged that little of use can be recovered of the early life. Watt and Bernard Lewis rejected the idea that he was a deliberate impostor, and Lewis held that Islam denounced aristocratic privilege and opened careers to talent. European writers from Postel to Carlyle assessed him very differently, from sage lawgiver to, in Voltaire's play, a symbol of fanaticism.

summary: Muhammad (c. 570 to 632) was born in Mecca, reported revelations from about 610 and led his followers to Medina in 622. By his death most of Arabia had accepted Islam. Muslims hold him to be the final prophet; historians study him through sources written later.
